1254.title: The Seers Who Heard the Vedas
1254.hook: who wrote the Vedas? the creation hymn shows the seers at work, stretching a line across the dark
1254.carry: the vedas were heard by seers, not invented
1254.tomorrow: even the gods came later. so who really knows how it began?
1254.howItsDone: Hindus call the Vedas shruti, 'what was heard' by the rishis, and keep them by chanting learned from a teacher; the Nasadiya Sukta's fifth verse is read in more than one way by commentators and modern readers.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth verse of the Nasadiya Sukta: kama, desire, the first seed of mind, and poets searching their hearts for the bond of what is in what is not.
screen: `KAMA, THE FIRST SEED OF MIND.`

segments.voice: Who wrote the Vedas? Ask a Hindu grandmother and you may get a surprising answer: nobody wrote them. They were heard. Yesterday the Rig Veda's creation hymn showed poets searching their hearts for where everything came from, and finding the bond of what is in what is not. Today's verse shows what those seers did next. They stretched a line across the dark, and then, right away, they asked about it.
screen: `WHO WROTE THE VEDAS?` → `POETS SEARCHING THEIR HEARTS.` → `A LINE ACROSS THE DARK.`

segments.voice: The fifth verse of the Nasadiya Sukta, in paraphrase: their cord was stretched across. Was there something below it? Was there something above it? There were seed-placers, there were great powers: their own power below, a giving forth above. The word for cord is rashmi: a ray, a rein, a line. Whose cord? The verse says only 'their'. Many readers take it to be the poets of the verse before, the ones who searched their hearts, so their insight is the line drawn across the dark. And even while they describe, they ask: was there below? was there above? Here a big Hindu teaching comes into view. Hindus call the Vedas shruti, what was heard. Tradition calls the rishis seers of the mantras: they didn't invent the hymns at a desk, they saw and heard them in deep attention, and handed them on mouth to ear, teacher to student, sound for sound. That's why the Vedas were kept by chanting for many centuries before anyone relied on writing them down, and why a family still calls a pandit who learned them by heart. In this verse you can watch the seers at work: looking inward, drawing a line, and honestly asking about both sides. It's the same reason a child in a Hindu home often learns a prayer by ear from a grandparent long before she can read it. So when a friend asks who wrote your scripture, here's a Hindu answer: in our telling, seers heard it, and we keep it by sound.
screen: `RASHMI: A CORD, A RAY, A LINE.` · `WAS THERE BELOW? WAS THERE ABOVE?` · `SHRUTI: HANDED ON MOUTH TO EAR.` · `SEERS HEARD IT; WE KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Vedic recitation traditionally begins with Om, so begin there. Sit easily and chant Om softly three times, or say it in your mind, letting the sound fade each time; then sit in the quiet after it and listen, the way the seers are pictured listening, not making anything up, just hearing. If you pray, let the quiet be prayer; if you don't, simply listen.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its fifth verse, the seers stretch a line across the dark, and ask about both sides of it.
screen: `THE NASADIYA SUKTA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Vedas were heard by seers, not invented. And even their line got a question on each side. See you tomorrow.

1255.title: Who Really Knows?
1255.hook: the creation hymn says even the gods came later, and ends on a question. in hinduism, asking is part of the path
1255.carry: in hinduism, asking is part of believing
1255.tomorrow: a person with a thousand heads. who is he?
1255.howItsDone: Hindu commentators and modern readers hear the Nasadiya Sukta's closing 'or perhaps does not know' in different ways; the hymn is still kept in Vedic recitation, and inquiry (jijnasa) is honored as a path in Hindu teaching.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's fifth verse: a cord stretched across, and a question asked on each side of it.
screen: `A CORD STRETCHED ACROSS.`

segments.voice: Where was I before I was born? A small child might ask it at bedtime, wide awake, while the grown-up in the doorway searches for an answer. There are a few ways to handle it. Give a confident answer. Change the subject. Or sit on the edge of the bed and say, honestly, that's a big one, and nobody has seen all the way back. The Nasadiya Sukta has circled a bigger version of that question since its first verse. In its last two, it asks it straight out.
screen: `WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?` → `A CONFIDENT ANSWER, OR A NEW SUBJECT?` → `OR: NOBODY HAS SEEN THAT FAR BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse six opens with a question. Ko addha veda. Who really knows? Who here could declare it, where this was born, where this creation came from? Then a startling line. The gods, it says, came after this world's making. So even the gods weren't there to see the start. Who, then, knows where it arose? Verse seven tries one more answer. Whether it was made or not, the one who watches over it in the highest heaven surely knows. And then the hymn's last words: or perhaps that one does not know. So anga veda yadi va na veda. Some traditional readers hear reverence there: the beginning is so deep only the highest could know it. Some modern readers hear honest doubt, kept inside scripture. And this is a big Hindu teaching, hiding in plain sight: asking is part of the path. The Brahma Sutras, the classic summary of the Upanishads' teaching, open with one line: athato brahma jijnasa. Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Not now, believe. Now, ask. Arjuna spends much of the Bhagavad Gita asking Krishna questions, and Krishna answers. So for many Hindus doubt isn't faith's enemy; it's how faith goes deeper. If someone tells you religion is only answers and science is only questions, the Rig Veda's own creation hymn ends with a question mark, and it is still chanted.
screen: `KO ADDHA VEDA: WHO REALLY KNOWS?` · `THE GODS CAME AFTER THE MAKING.` · `OR PERHAPS DOES NOT KNOW.` · `JIJNASA: NOW, ASK.`

segments.voice: Bring up one thing you know because you were there, a face, a kitchen, a street you walked, and silently call it seen; then something you only believe, or were told, or wonder about, and call it not seen, gently, with no judgment. Go back and forth for a while, noticing that both can be held in the same quiet mind; if you pray, bring one not-seen to God as an honest question, the way Arjuna did.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. It ends: the one in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps that one does not know.
screen: `THE NASADIYA SUKTA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in Hinduism, asking is part of believing. Even the creation hymn ends, who really knows? Tomorrow: who has a thousand heads?

1256.title: A Thousand Heads
1256.hook: a person with a thousand heads who is all this and still more: the Veda's first picture of god in everything
1256.carry: god is in all this, every face included
1256.tomorrow: if god is everything, is everything all of god?
1256.howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting; its 'the Purusha is all this' is one root of the Hindu teaching that the divine is present in everything, which many Hindus connect with namaste.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta ended: the one in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps does not know.
screen: `OR PERHAPS DOES NOT KNOW.`

segments.voice: A festival crowd, photographed from a rooftop. At first it looks like one moving surface. Then you zoom in. Heads, thousands of them. Hands in the air. Sandals, a child on someone's shoulders. One crowd, and countless people, and you can't quite say where one ends and the next begins. The Rig Veda has a hymn that opens on a picture like that, except the crowd is one person, and the person is bigger than the world. After a hymn that asked who knows, here's one that begins by describing.
screen: `A CROWD FROM A ROOFTOP.` → `ONE THING, COUNTLESS PEOPLE.` → `NOW MAKE IT ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Purusha means person. Here, in the Rig Veda, it names a cosmic person, and the hymn opens: sahasra-shirsha purushah. The Purusha has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. Many readers hear thousand as beyond counting: every head is in some sense his, every pair of eyes, every step. He covered the earth on every side, and stood beyond it by ten fingers' width. Not a mountain more: ten fingers. Then verse two: purusha eva idam sarvam. The Purusha is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be. This is one of the oldest seeds of a teaching Hindus carry everywhere: the divine isn't somewhere else, behind the sky. It's here, in all this. The Upanishads say it again later, sarvam khalv idam brahma, all this is Brahman. And many Hindus explain their everyday greeting the same way: the folded hands of namaste bow to the divine in the person in front of you. So that rooftop crowd isn't a mass of strangers. On the hymn's picture, every face in it is one of the thousand. Next time you're squeezed into a crowded train or a packed school hallway, that's the Purusha Sukta's view: one sacred person, looking out through all those eyes. And still, ten fingers more.
screen: `PURUSHA: A PERSON.` · `A THOUSAND HEADS, EYES AND FEET.` · `PURUSHA EVA IDAM SARVAM: ALL THIS.` · `NAMASTE: BOWING TO THE DIVINE IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three faces you'll see today: someone you love, someone you pass without noticing, someone who's hard for you. Fold your hands at your chest, and for each one, bow a little, inwardly, the way namaste does. If you pray, see the divine looking out through their eyes; if you don't, simply wish each of them well.
The Purusha Sukta. The hymn of the cosmic person: a thousand heads, eyes and feet, all that has been and will be, and still ten fingers more.

1257.title: The Quarter We Can See
1257.hook: the whole world, every star and ant, is one quarter of the cosmic person. why hindus see god in nature without calling nature all of god

1257.tomorrow: what was the world made from?
1257.howItsDone: Hindu teachers cite the Purusha Sukta's 'a quarter of him is all beings' and the Gita's 'a single fragment' when speaking of the divine as present in the world and also beyond it; the hymn is recited in Vedic chanting.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, god is in all this, every face included opened: a person with a thousand heads, covering the earth and standing beyond it by ten fingers' width.
screen: `A THOUSAND HEADS, AND TEN FINGERS MORE.`

segments.voice: Someone you've worked beside for years, the one who fixes the printer and remembers birthdays, stands up at a wedding and sings. The room goes quiet, because the voice is extraordinary. You had no idea. You knew a real part of this person, nothing fake about it. But it was a part, and not the larger one. The Purusha Sukta's third verse does something like that with the whole world. It takes everything that exists, every star and ant and city, and says: this is the part of him you've met.
screen: `THE COWORKER WHO FIXES THE PRINTER.` → `THEN SHE SINGS.` → `YOU'D ONLY MET A PART.`

segments.voice: Verse three: such is his greatness, and the Purusha is greater still. Then a proportion. Pado asya vishva bhutani. A quarter of him is all beings. Pada means a foot, and also a quarter. Everything that lives and dies is one quarter. Three quarters of him, the verse says, are immortal, in heaven. Verse four goes on. With three quarters the Purusha rose up. The one quarter came to be here, again and again, and from it he spread out into what eats and what doesn't: the hungry sparrow and the stone. So the world, for all its size, is the smaller share. Every galaxy, every person, is truly his, and still only the part that came down. Later Hindu texts keep this shape. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna he holds up this whole universe with a single fragment of himself. Scholars sometimes call this panentheism: everything is in God, and God is more than everything. It's why a Hindu can bow to a river, a tree, a cow, a teacher, and still pray to a God no river could hold. So if someone says Hindus just worship nature, the oldest layer of the Veda answers: nature is sacred because it's his, and it's the quarter we can see.
screen: `SUCH IS HIS GREATNESS, AND MORE.` · `PADA: A FOOT, A QUARTER.` · `ALL BEINGS ARE ONE QUARTER.` · `IN GOD, AND GOD IS MORE.`

segments.voice: Look at one living thing near you, a plant, a pet, the sky in a window, or picture one. Let it be sacred, part of the quarter that came down, and touch your hands together toward it. Then close your eyes and rest in what's beyond it, the three quarters no eye has seen. If you pray, pray to the One who is more; if you don't, simply rest in the more.
The Purusha Sukta. In its third and fourth verses, all beings are one quarter of the Purusha, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.

1258.title: The World Born From an Offering
1258.hook: in the Purusha Sukta the world comes from an offering. it's why hindus offer food to god before they eat it
1258.carry: offer it first: the world began as giving
1258.tomorrow: does the Rig Veda rank people by birth?
1258.howItsDone: Hindus offer ghee into the sacred fire in a havan and offer food before a murti in puja, then receive it as prasad; the Purusha Sukta's first offering and the Gita's teaching on yajna stand behind the practice.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, God is in all this, every face included, and the proportion: all beings are one quarter of him, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.
screen: `ALL BEINGS: ONE QUARTER.`

segments.voice: What would you make a world out of? Clay, shaped by a potter's hands, is one answer. A spoken word is another. A seed, a shell, a cosmic egg: people have told it more than one way. The Purusha Sukta's answer comes from the fire ritual the hymn itself describes, where offerings are poured into a flame. In this hymn the world comes from an offering, and the ingredients aren't butter and wood. They're spring, summer and autumn.
screen: `CLAY? A WORD? A SEED?` → `THE HYMN'S ANSWER: AN OFFERING.` → `THE INGREDIENTS ARE SEASONS.`

segments.voice: The word is yajna, an offering poured into fire in Vedic worship. Verse six says that when the gods performed a yajna with the Purusha as the offering, spring was its melted butter, summer its fuel, autumn the offering itself. The year itself, poured into the flame. Verse seven: on the sacred grass they sprinkled him, the one born in the beginning. From that offering, fully given, came the creatures of the air, the forest and the village. Verse nine: from it were born the verses and the chants, the meters and formulas, the Vedas themselves. A hymn telling where hymns come from. So in this telling the world isn't built from outside like a house. It comes from something given. And here's what Hindus do because of it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says beings were created together with yajna, and that the good who eat what remains of the offering are freed from fault, while those who cook only for themselves eat wrong. So Hindus offer first: ghee poured into the havan fire, a plate set before the murti, and only then is it eaten, as prasad, the gift that comes back. Many families say a line from the Gita before meals for the same reason. If the world began as giving, then eating is joining in, not just taking.

1259.title: The Varna Verse
1259.hook: one verse names four groups from one body. it has been used to rank people by birth, and fought over ever since
1259.carry: one body, and careful hands for a hard verse
1259.tomorrow: where did the moon come from?
1259.howItsDone: Hindus read the Purusha Sukta's verse on the four groups in sharply different ways: some as the origin of the varnas, others as a picture of one interdependent body, and reformers have challenged its use to justify caste by birth.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, God fills the world and is still more. Then the great offering: spring as butter, summer as fuel, autumn as the offering, and from it creatures, chants and verses.
screen: `A WORLD THAT COMES FROM GIVING.`

segments.voice: When they divided the Purusha, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth? What were his arms? What are his thighs and feet called? That's the Purusha Sukta's eleventh verse, in paraphrase, nothing but questions, like a teacher quizzing a class. The answer comes in the next verse. It's short, and it has been recited, defended and fought over. You met the caste question on day ninety-five, and in the Gita on day two hundred twenty-two. Today, the verse itself.
screen: `WHAT WAS HIS MOUTH? HIS ARMS?` → `A VERSE OF QUESTIONS.` → `AN ANSWER THAT'S BEEN FOUGHT OVER.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve answers, in paraphrase: the brahmin, the priest, was his mouth. His arms were made the rajanya, the ruler and warrior. His thighs became the vaishya, the people of trade and farming. From his feet the shudra, the laborer, was born. Four groups, from one body. Notice the wording. The verse doesn't use the word varna, the later word for these social orders, and it doesn't say higher or lower. But readers have heard a ranking in mouth and feet, and that's where the argument begins. Some traditional readers take the verse as the sacred origin of the four varnas. Over time it was also used to defend a ladder fixed by birth, and people outside the four orders altogether were treated as untouchable. Reformers, among them B. R. Ambedkar, attacked that use of the verse directly and fought the system it was used to defend. Other readers, Hindu teachers among them, stress that all four come from one body, and point to the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says the four orders were made according to qualities and actions, arguing birth was never meant to decide them. These readings don't agree, and this path won't pretend they do. India's constitution abolished untouchability in 1950, and many Hindus today reject any ranking by birth. If a friend asks you about caste, you can say what the text says, what people did with it, and who was hurt. A verse can be held sacred and still need careful hands.
screen: `MOUTH, ARMS, THIGHS, FEET.` · `ONE BODY. THE WORD VARNA ISN'T THERE.` · `A LADDER BY BIRTH, AND ITS CRITICS.` · `QUALITIES AND ACTIONS, NOT BIRTH?`

segments.voice: Give each part of the body the same few breaths: the mouth, lips and tongue resting; the arms and hands; the thighs, their weight on the chair; and the feet, which carry everything and are usually noticed least. No part gets more; if you pray, you can pray for anyone who has been treated as less.
The Purusha Sukta. In its twelfth verse, mouth, arms, thighs and feet become four groups of people, and readers have argued over what that means ever since.

1260.title: The Moon From His Mind
1260.hook: the moon from the cosmic person's mind, the sun from his eye, and in the Upanishad they come back to live in you
1260.carry: you are a small copy of the cosmos
1260.tomorrow: with the offering, the gods offered to the offering. what were the first dharmas?
1260.howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting, and its picture of the world fashioned from the cosmic person's body is mirrored in the Aitareya Upanishad, where the world's powers enter the human body.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, offer it first: the world began as giving. Then the hardest verse: mouth, arms, thighs and feet as four groups, and the honest argument over what that means.
screen: `ONE BODY, AND AN HONEST ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: The moon was born from his mind. That's a line from the Purusha Sukta, in paraphrase, and it comes with a whole list. The sun, from his eye. The wind, from his breath. The sky, from his head. Look up some clear night and try reading the sky that way: not as a ceiling, but as a face, a breath, a mind, far bigger than yours and somehow related to yours. The hymn has turned from the people of the world to the world itself, and it draws the map with a body.
screen: `THE MOON, FROM HIS MIND.` → `THE SUN, FROM HIS EYE.` → `A SKY MADE FROM A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen begins chandrama manaso jatah: the moon, born from mind. From his eye, the sun. From his mouth, Indra and Agni, the god of storm and the god of fire. From his breath, Vayu, the wind. Verse fourteen goes on. From his navel, the middle air. From his head, the sky took shape. From his feet, the earth. From his ear, the directions. And so, it says, they fashioned the worlds. Listen to how the pairs fit. Eye and sun: light and seeing. Breath and wind: the same moving air, small and large. Feet and earth: what stands, and what is stood on. Earlier on this path, the Aitareya Upanishad told the same story in reverse: fire became speech and entered the mouth, wind became breath and entered the nose, the sun became sight and entered the eyes, the moon became mind and entered the heart. Together they make a loop, and a big Hindu teaching: the cosmos is a vast person, and a person is a small cosmos. What lights the sky lights your eyes; what moves the trees moves your breath. Many teachers draw from it a reason to treat the body with reverence, as a home the powers of the world came to live in. So on a full-moon night, the hymn invites you to look up and see not just a rock in the sky, but a mind, kin to the one that's looking.
screen: `MIND TO MOON, EYE TO SUN.` · `BREATH TO WIND, FEET TO EARTH.` · `THE AITAREYA: THE SAME, IN REVERSE.` · `A PERSON IS A SMALL COSMOS.`

segments.voice: Feel the breath at the nostrils and let it be wind for a moment; notice light through closed eyelids and let it be the sun; feel the feet on the floor and let it be the earth; listen for sounds from every side. Then rest the mind and let it be as quiet as the moon, going slowly, body, then world, then body again; if you pray, you can pray there.
The Purusha Sukta. In verses thirteen and fourteen, mind becomes the moon, eye the sun, breath the wind, feet the earth, and so the worlds are fashioned.
